candidate_targets: individuals struggling with relationship control issues
people seeking to clarify personal values in relationships
clients aiming to improve interpersonal behavior
contraindications: May be less effective or potentially frustrating for individuals with severe control issues or those unable to accept personal responsibility; caution with clients who may misinterpret focus on self as blame.
original_extraction.evidence_text:
5. What sort of ongoing activities do you want to do with your partner?

---

Youll notice that these are virtually identical to the first set of questions. Again, they’re all about
how you want to be, not about how you want your partner to be. Why? Because in any relationship,
you only have control over one person and that’s you. How your partner behaves is up to your

---

partner. Of course, it is in your control to request changes from your partner and to set boundaries
on what you will and won’t accept. And as I said, this will be far more effective if you’re behaving
as the ‘ideal you’. These same principles apply to all the relationships you have with friends,
family, colleagues, employees and anyone you'll ever meet! Remember the golden rule: treat
others as you’d like them to treat you.

---

Sometimes, as a response to the above questions, my clients jot downa long list of the qualities
they’re looking for in a partner. But in describing the sort of partner you want, you’re describing a
goal. To get to your values in this domain, you need to ask, “If I did find the partner I want, how
would I like to be in that relationship? What personal qualities would I like to bring to it?’ (Of
course, it can be very useful to think about the sort of partner you’d like—but that’s not what this
exercise is about.)

---

2. If you could be the ‘ideal you’, how would you behave toward your friends?

---

3. What personal qualities would you like to bring to these friendships?

---

4. What sort of friendships do you want to build?

---

5. What sort of ongoing activities do you want to do with your friends?

---

Once again, these questions focus on what’s in your control: how you behave as a friend. If you’ve
written about the sort of friends you’d like, that’s useful. You can set yourself a goal to go out and
meet people like that. But to clarify your values on friendship, you need to ask yourself, ‘What sort
of friend would I like to be?’
generation_rules: Focus questions on how the individual wants to be in relationships, not on how others should be
Encourage reflection on personal qualities to bring to relationships
Promote setting boundaries based on one’s own behavior as the ideal self
pause_rules: Allow reflective pauses after questions to enable introspection on personal values and behaviors.
original_extraction.psychological_function: Facilitates acceptance of personal responsibility and control, reduces frustration from trying to change others, and supports development of ideal self-concept in social contexts.
repetition_rules: Repeat focus on self-behavior and personal qualities across different relationship contexts to reinforce internal locus of control.
symbolic_elements: golden rule: treat others as you’d like them to treat you
original_extraction.therapeutic_function: Encourages individuals to focus on their own behavior and personal qualities in relationships rather than attempting to control others, promoting self-awareness and value clarification.
voice_rules: Maintain a supportive and non-judgmental tone
